props.title: Everyone Else
props.initialSlug: Young couple's vacation exposes relationship cracks

sections.content: Everyone Else (2009) stands as a masterwork of modern German relationship cinema, director Maren Ade's unflinching examination of a couple unraveling during a Sardinian vacation. Like Bergman's Scenes from a Marriage (1973), it captures the microscopic fissures that eventually crack a relationship wide open. The film's power lies in its acute observation of how Chris (Lars Eidinger) and Gitti (Birgit Minichmayr) perform for each other, echoing the relationship dynamics seen in Force Majeure (2014) and 45 Years (2015).

sections.content: Ade's approach to relationship dysfunction influenced a wave of European intimate dramas that followed. Like Blue Valentine (2010) and Marriage Story (2019), the film excels in showing how partners can simultaneously love and destroy each other. The vacation setting serves as both paradise and prison, reminiscent of how L'Avventura (1960) used Mediterranean landscapes to heighten emotional isolation.

The film's genius lies in its treatment of class and ambition. Chris's architectural career and his encounter with a more successful colleague create a pressure cooker of professional jealousy and personal inadequacy. This theme of career anxiety poisoning romance echoes through later works like The Worst Person in the World (2021) and Past Lives (2023). SUBHEAD: Modern Relationship Cinema's Evolution

sections.content: Everyone Else helped establish a new language for depicting modern relationships, where external success and internal fulfillment create unbearable tension. The film's influence can be seen in works like The Lost Daughter (2021) and Bergman Island (2021), where professional and personal identities clash in sun-drenched settings that belie darker emotional currents.
